paragraphs.heading: Two operations on one set
paragraphs.text: A ring is a set with two operations, usually called addition and multiplication and written the way we write them for integers. They behave much like adding and multiplying integers, with one big difference: multiplication in a ring need not be commutative, so ab may differ from ba. The elements can be numbers such as integers or complex numbers. They can also be things that are not numbers at all, like polynomials, square matrices, functions and power series.

paragraphs.heading: The rules
paragraphs.text: Under addition, a ring is an abelian group. Addition is associative and commutative, there is a 0 with a + 0 = a, and each a has a −a with a + (−a) = 0. Multiplication is associative and has an identity 1, with a · 1 = a and 1 · a = a. The operations are tied together on both sides: a · (b + c) = (a · b) + (a · c) and (b + c) · a = (b · a) + (c · a). These axioms are modelled on familiar facts about adding and multiplying integers.

paragraphs.heading: What a ring may lack
paragraphs.text: A ring does not have to contain multiplicative inverses. A nonzero ring where every nonzero element has an inverse is called a division ring; if it is also commutative, it is a field. Many authors also drop the requirement of a 1; a structure that meets every other axiom but has no 1 is called a rng, a ring with the "i" taken out. The even integers with the usual + and ⋅ are a rng, not a ring.

paragraphs.heading: Commutative or not
paragraphs.text: Rings whose multiplication is commutative, like the integers, are called commutative rings. Other examples are every field, polynomials in one or several variables, and the ring of integers of a number field. Their theory, commutative algebra, is a major branch of ring theory; it grew under the influence of algebraic number theory and algebraic geometry and is now a basic tool in both. Noncommutative examples include real square matrices of size n × n with n ≥ 2, group rings, rings of differential operators and cohomology rings in topology.

paragraphs.heading: Quick consequences
paragraphs.text: Several facts follow straight from the axioms. Zero absorbs everything under multiplication, x0 = 0 = 0x, and (–1)x = –x. If 0 = 1 in a ring, the ring has just one element and is called the zero ring. The binomial formula still holds for any x and y with xy = yx. Even the commutativity of addition can be derived from the other axioms, with the help of the 1.

paragraphs.heading: A small example
paragraphs.text: In the ring ℤ/4ℤ, the sum x̄ + ȳ is the remainder left when the integer x + y is divided by 4. So 2̄ + 3̄ = 1̄, and 3̄ + 3̄ = 2̄.

paragraphs.heading: Where rings came from
paragraphs.text: The idea of a ring took shape between the 1870s and the 1920s, with major work from Richard Dedekind, David Hilbert, Abraham Fraenkel and Emmy Noether. Rings were first formalized to generalize Dedekind domains from number theory, along with polynomial rings and rings of invariants from algebraic geometry and invariant theory. Later they proved useful in other parts of mathematics, such as geometry and analysis.
